text:
Primary schools should keep teaching joined-up handwriting, and the case rests on a simple observation: most of the arguments for dropping it are really arguments against teaching it badly, and the benefits of teaching it well are larger and more durable than its critics allow.

Start with the strongest form of the opposing view, because it deserves a fair hearing. Children now grow up surrounded by screens, adults rarely write more than a shopping list or a signature by hand, and exams are slowly migrating to laptops. Teaching cursive, the critics say, is a nostalgic ritual, like teaching children to darn socks or write with a nib. Classroom time is finite, and every hour spent on looping letter-joins is an hour not spent on reading, mathematics or, for that matter, typing. Some education systems have already acted on this logic. Finland, to take the best-known case, removed any requirement to teach cursive in its national core curriculum a decade ago, with schools free to choose, and the sky did not fall. If a country that tops so many league tables can shrug off joined writing, why should anyone else cling to it?

The first reply is that the premise about the future is shakier than it looks. Handwriting is not disappearing from adult life; it is changing its role. People still take notes in meetings, fill in forms, annotate documents, write cards, label things and jot down a phone number when the battery is dead. Pupils still sit examinations in which they must write by hand, often at speed, for hours, and the quality of that handwriting affects how their work is read and marked. A child who cannot write quickly and legibly is not liberated by the existence of keyboards; she is disadvantaged in precisely the high-stakes moments when it matters most. Typing and handwriting are complementary skills, not rivals, and a competent adult needs both.

The second reply concerns speed, which is the central practical argument for joining letters. Printing letters one at a time means lifting the pen after every stroke, whereas joined writing lets the hand travel in a continuous flow, with fewer stops and starts, and makes the shapes of letters more economical. This is no trivial refinement: when the physical act of writing is slow and effortful, it competes with the thinking that the writing is supposed to express. A child who has to concentrate on forming each letter has less attention left for choosing the right word, organising an argument or remembering what she meant to say next. Researchers who study writing development, Virginia Berninger among the best known, have long reported that children whose handwriting is fluent and automatic tend to write longer and better compositions than those whose handwriting is laboured. Since automaticity frees the mind, teaching a fluent joined hand is not decoration on top of literacy; it is part of the machinery that lets children get their ideas onto the page.

There is a fair objection here, and I should concede its force. Plenty of adults who write quickly and legibly do not use textbook cursive at all. Their hands settle into a personal blend of print and joins, and studies of adult handwriting suggest this hybrid is common and works perfectly well. Nobody needs to produce the exact loops of a copybook alphabet to function, but this point cuts in favour of teaching joined writing, not against it, because the hybrid hand that adults develop is built on a foundation. Children who are taught a consistent joined style, and who practise it until it is fluent, arrive at their own efficient adult hand through a sound route, while children who are taught nothing in particular tend to arrive at a muddle, with letters formed in inconsistent ways, unnecessary lifts of the pen and a hand that tires quickly. The structured teaching of joins is scaffolding, and although adults may modify the building later, they are better off having had it.

The third argument is about what handwriting does for the developing brain, and here I want to be careful not to overclaim. The evidence is suggestive rather than conclusive, but it points in a consistent direction. In a well-known study by Karin James and colleagues, young children who learned letters by drawing them by hand showed more activity in brain regions associated with reading than children who learned the same letters by typing or tracing. Other work has found that handwriting letters helps children recognise and remember them. The act of forming a shape with the hand, with all its small variations and its demands on coordination, appears to leave a richer trace than pressing a key. This research is mostly about handwriting in general, not joined handwriting in particular, and I would not pretend otherwise, but it establishes the principle that writing by hand is not merely a slow way of doing what a keyboard does quickly. The skills are different, and the hand-based one seems to support early literacy. If we accept that children should learn to write by hand at all, the question becomes which hand to teach, and the answer that supports fluency is a joined one.

A related and often-cited finding concerns note-taking. Pam Mueller and Daniel Oppenheimer reported in 2014 that students who took lecture notes by hand did better on conceptual questions than those who typed, apparently because handwriting forces you to summarise rather than transcribe. Later attempts to replicate this have produced mixed results, and I think honesty requires saying that the finding is contested. Still, the broad intuition behind it is plausible: slower, more deliberate recording encourages processing. For a primary school child, whose task is to build the habit of turning thought into language, a medium that rewards that kind of engagement is worth protecting.

The fourth argument is about inclusion, and it is where the opposing view is most often thought to be strongest and is in fact weakest. Some pupils, notably many with dyslexia or dyspraxia, struggle with handwriting, and it is sometimes argued that cursive makes things harder for them. For some individual children that may be true, and schools should always be flexible, allowing keyboards and other adjustments where they genuinely help. But there is also a respectable body of practitioner opinion holding that joined writing can be easier for children who reverse letters, because the continuous movement gives each word a single motor pattern and makes it harder to confuse letters such as b and d. The honest conclusion is that no single approach suits every child, which is an argument for teaching the mainstream skill well and adapting for the exceptions, not for abandoning the skill for everyone.

Finally, there is a cultural point that I do not think should be dismissed as sentimentality. Handwriting is how we read our own history: letters, diaries, marginal notes, wartime postcards and the scrawled recipe from a grandmother are all written in joined script. A child who cannot read cursive is cut off from a large part of the written record of her own family and society, and will need an interpreter for documents that her great-grandparents wrote without a second thought. Handwriting is also a personal signature in a broader sense, a way of making a mark that is recognisably yours, and it is reasonable to want children to have that, even in an age of uniform fonts.

What follows from all this is not that schools should simply carry on as before. The real weakness in many classrooms is not that cursive is taught but how. Too often it is taught late, in a rush, with worksheets and little coaching, by teachers who were never trained in it themselves, and then abandoned the moment children reach secondary school, and a child taught this way will indeed come to see it as a pointless chore. The remedy is better teaching: short, frequent, well-modelled practice in the early years, a clear and consistent style across the school, attention to posture and pencil grip, and a sensible handover to the pupil's own developing hand as she gets older. Expecting every child to produce flawless copybook script would be a mistake; expecting every child to leave primary school able to write legibly, comfortably and at a reasonable speed is not.

So the choice is not between an old-fashioned tradition and a modern world. It is between giving children a fluent, adaptable skill that supports their thinking, their exam performance and their access to the past, and leaving them to pick up something half-formed on their own. Typing will take care of itself, since children will learn it from the devices that surround them whether or not we teach it, but handwriting will not, and it needs deliberate instruction, of which joined-up writing, taught well, is the most efficient form. Primary schools should keep teaching it, and should teach it better.
